native_result.query: How does the effect of increasing education expenditure on per capita GDP compare between developing countries and countries in Sub-Saharan Africa?
native_result.HypoA: The effect of increasing education expenditure on per capita GDP is more pronounced in developing countries outside of Sub-Saharan Africa compared to those within it
native_result.HypoB: Increasing government education expenditure (% of GNI) is positively associated with subsequent (≈2-yr lagged) per-capita GDP, and the effect is larger and more robustly positive in Sub-Saharan Africa than in lower-middle-income/developing countries: in SSA a 1pp rise in education spending is associated with ≈+4.6pp per-capita GNI growth (interaction vs LMC p≈0.02) and ≈+6.9–7.5pp of export/output-proxy growth (p<0.05); in LMC the association is near zero and imprecise. The between-group difference is significant on the direct per-capita GDP measure but not on the balanced export-output comparison (interaction p≈0.3–0.8); SSA per-capita GDP covers only 2011–2015, so the comparison is directional and robustly positive for SSA rather than a firmly established larger effect.
native_result.WorkflowB: Wide-to-long reshape (group×year panel 1975–2015); missingness audit; descriptive + lead-lag correlation analysis (edu at lags 0–5 vs GNI level, ΔlogGNI, exports growth) per group; primary comparison = pooled balanced-window (1991–2015) regressions with SSA×edu interaction on exports-growth output proxy, plus direct Δlog(per-capita GNI) model; per-group time-series OLS (full & parsimonious, Newey-West HAC), AR(1) term for autoregression, time trend; robustness: lag sensitivity (L1–L3), no-trend, LMC 1975–2015 long window; diagnostics: Ljung-Box residual autocorrelation, residual AR(1), VIF. Associative/quasi-causal interpretation only (no instruments; 2 aggregate units).
